messages.subject: Differences in inference when using different algorithms and different versions of INLA
parts:
Dear all,

I have been noticing some differences in inference when using different algorithms and different versions of INLA. I have two questions relating to the classic and compact algorithms in INLA 23.09.09 and INLA 24.02.09. I used an example and R code of species distribution modelling using spatial point processes from https://www.paulamoraga.com/tutorial-point-patterns/. My experimental runs showed that the intercept estimates between the classic and compact are quite different in INLA 23.09.09. The classic algorithm gives negative values, close to the value posted on https://www.paulamoraga.com/tutorial-point-patterns/ and the paper  (https://journal.r-project.org/archive/2021/RJ-2021-017/RJ-2021-017.pdf), but the compact algorithm gives positive values. However, in INLA 24.02.09, the classic algorithm carries out positive estimates larger than the estimates presented by the compact algorithm. The info inside INLA NEWS.md makes it hard for me to identify what causes the performance of the classic algorithm to be different between INLA 23.09.09 and INLA 24.02.09. In terms of model prediction, I think that the inferences between the two INLA versions could be quite different, which is worrying. I understand the algorithm is evolving and improving. However, I am still concerned about the difference and unsure which version is reliable. Are there key tuning arguments in function "inla" which can make the classic algorithms in the two INLA versions produce comparable outcomes? For our real data, which can't be shared, the intercepts are very important and these differences from algorithms are difficult to navigate. Any advice is warmly welcomed.

The other question is about the compact algorithm (i.e. the default algorithm). Warning messages about vb.correction were popped up when the model fitting was conducted in Linux systems (i.e. WSL Ubuntu). However, the warning was not given when the fitting was conducted in the Windows system. Does this mean that vb.correction was successful in the Windows runs?

I am attaching a zip file containing the R scripts and the results of my experimental runs. Inside the zip file, folders inla23.09.09 and inla24.02.09 include the R script and my experimental results (i.e. Rout) produced by inla23.09.09 and inla24.02.09, respectively. The R script was run three times in the Windows system and three times in the Linux system. The Rout files provide the profile of R versions and packages. Note that both folders inla23.09.09 and inla24.02.09 are an renv project (https://rstudio.github.io/renv/articles/renv.html). Open an R session inside the folder for the first time, and the renv should automatically install the packages used in the R script. However, because INLA is unavailable on the R CRAN, sill need to install INLA manually. Although not 100%, the renv should create a similar R environment.  

   
Thank you.

Best
Wen-Hsi

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Differences in inference when using different algorithms and different versions of INLA
parts:
Hi,
Without looking at your code&results, but only looking at the point process example you linked to, I can say that in that example the intercept is _massively_ non-identifiable, likely due to confounding with the 2d rw2 model. For any such model, you need to carefully consider what actual property of the model that is of interest.
Firstly, in the example, if you (for example) are interested in the integral over space of the intensity function, that cannot be extracted from the intercept parameter alone, but is instead a nonlinear function of the entire model, so you should not rely on the intercept parameter estimate. The easiest approach is instead to use posterior sampling, and compute the quantity of interest for each sample; this gives you a sample from the posterior distribution of that quantity, so that you can estimate the posterior mean and quantiles from that, without relying on summary statistics of the individual posterior distributions for the model parameters directly.
Secondly, when the intercept is that much nonidentifiable, it is likely that the numerical point estimate is sensitive to small details in the model definition and numerical optimisation method, which again means that you need to consider what aggregate model property you’re really interested in, and if that property _is_ reliably estimable. For example, the sum of the intercept and random field components is likely to be more identifiable than either component on its own. So in order to determine whether the different methods give _meaningfully_ different estimates, you need to compare model properties that are reliably estimable, and not focus on nonidentifiable model parameters.
Finn

Hi Finn,

Thank you for your responses. I have some follow-up questions.
 
 1) Can you explain where the confounding comes from? The model is quite simple (i.e. intercept + a linear covariate + random effect). It is unclear how the intercept confounds with the 2d rw2 model. Is the intercept embedded in the 2d rw2 model?

 2) Would things change with an SPDE approach? I am currently modifying the example code to test it.

 3) We used the sloth data as an example. In our real application (we can't easily share data), we are looking at integral over space (i.e. model prediction from a model with intercept, covariates and SPDE RE) instead of just inference from intercept. For this purpose, we will use posterior sampling to predict across space and integrate/sum over each of these predictions. Even so, the intercept is still a critical parameter for all predictions; hence it is crucial for the final integral. Despite the confounding, is it not sensible to be concerned that the intercept estimates vary too much with INLA versions and two algorithms?


Best,
Wen-Hsi

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Differences in inference when using different algorithms and different versions of INLA
parts:
By default the rw2 have a sum-to-zero constrain, which would make one think that it wouldn't be confounded with the intercept. However, the observations aren't equally spread across space (eg may be reatricted to a subset of space, or simply unevenly located). That means that one can "move" values between the rw2 model and the intercept, making the two components have posterior negative correlation on the observation locations. Their sum, which is what's relevant for i terrass across space of the predictor as a whole, is constrained by the observations, but the individual parameter much less. In other words, the intercept is _not_ the same as the spatial average.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Differences in inference when using different algorithms and different versions of INLA
parts:
Like I indicated before, if the posterior mode is flat or a flat ridge
(e.g. strong negative correlation between intercept and random field),
then the mode _will_ come out different depending on small details in
the numerical optimisation. The intercept is very rarely identifiable
on its own, so one should expect the details of the estimates to vary.
I would only care about quantities of interest, such as the combined
effect of the model components, and only in the region of interest.
The intercept by itself is usually _not_ interpretable in that sense.
Also, I would generally expect the more recent INLA versions to have
more accurate results, in particular when comparing with the "classic"
method. But _only_ if you look at identifiable properties;
unidentifiable properties are more sensitive to numerical details.
Finally, predictions that do involve the identifiable combinations of
model components are less sensitive to confounding issues (unless the
data collection and prediction setup is inherently confounding the
properties of interest; that's unrelated to how the results are
computed, and is a property of your data collection process and model
design.

Like I indicated before, if the posterior mode is flat or a flat ridge
(e.g. strong negative correlation between intercept and random field),
then the mode _will_ come out different depending on small details in
the numerical optimisation. The intercept is very rarely identifiable
on its own, so one should expect the details of the estimates to vary.
I would only care about quantities of interest, such as the combined
effect of the model components, and only in the region of interest.
The intercept by itself is usually _not_ interpretable in that sense.
Also, I would generally expect the more recent INLA versions to have
more accurate results, in particular when comparing with the "classic"
method. But _only_ if you look at identifiable properties;
unidentifiable properties are more sensitive to numerical details.
Finally, predictions that do involve the identifiable combinations of
model components are less sensitive to confounding issues (unless the
data collection and prediction setup is inherently confounding the
properties of interest; that's unrelated to how the results are
computed, and is a property of your data collection process and model
design.
Finn

Hi

I looked over the example concentrating on 'gorilla'

These are examples of models where the posterior almost flat, hence details
matters.

Like priors: for models with little data, you _have_ to be informative with
priors. that is precisions

I changed to

# P(sigma > 1) = 0.01
prior.sigma = c(0.3, 0.01))

and added

control.fixed = list(prec.intercept = 1),

constr=T for the spde will also do good.

the consequence of using non-informative priors is that internal correction
fail,

[1802] " *** Please (re-)consider your model, priors, confounding, etc."
[1803] " *** warning *** iterative process seems to diverge,
'vb.correction' is aborted"

these msg's is a clear sign that something is `not good'.

with the changes above, the compact mode runs without any issues and the DIC
values seems stable

btw, DIC values are notorious sensitive to small changes in the hyperparameters,
as its a sum, not a mean, hence you might tighten up the inner optimisation

control.inla = list(tolerance.step = 1e-8), 

or smaller. 


Older versions of INLA was less good in these cases, and therefore the optimizer
was improved to handle better these situations. (in the fall of 2023 sometime)

Also, there was a bug in the compact mode VB correction for the mean, where the
prior for fixed effects was not properly added, which was fixed here

# INLA 24.02.09
* Fixed a bug: prior means was not accounted for, doing the VB mean correction



the classic model is no longer suppored in the sense that no changes are done on
that part of code beyond bug-fixing (if that happens).



The compact mode is way better, both wrt speed and accuracy



If there is anything else, please let us know

H
